```{python}
#| label: setup-ada
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, accuracy_score
```

## Overview

**Boosting** is an ensemble method that builds models *sequentially*,
where each new model focuses on the examples the previous ones got wrong.
This differs from **bagging**, which builds trees *in parallel* on bootstrap samples and averages them.

AdaBoost uses **decision stumps**, a low variance, depth-1 trees. After each round, misclassified rows get *higher weight*
and correctly classified rows get *lower weight*,
so the next stump is forced to focus on hard cases. Each stump gets a **weight α** based on its weighted error:
$\alpha = \tfrac12 \ln\!\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon}$. So, a lower error means larger α. Predictions are combined as a
weighted vote $\hat y = \operatorname{sign}\!\big(\sum_t \alpha_t\, h_t(x)\big)$. Stumps that performed better have more say.

```{python}
#| label: fig-boosting-vs-bagging
#| fig-cap: "Bagging builds trees in parallel; AdaBoost builds them one after another, each new stump focused on previously misclassified rows."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9,3))

axes[0].set_title("Bagging (parallel)")
for i, xp in enumerate([0.15, 0.5, 0.85]):
    axes[0].add_patch(plt.Rectangle((xp-0.08, 0.55), 0.16, 0.25, fc="#cfe8ff", ec="k"))
    axes[0].text(xp, 0.675, f"tree {i+1}", ha="center", va="center")
    axes[0].annotate("", xy=(xp, 0.35), xytext=(xp, 0.55),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
axes[0].add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0.35, 0.05), 0.3, 0.2, fc="#ffe6b3", ec="k"))
axes[0].text(0.5, 0.15, "average", ha="center", va="center")
for xp in [0.15, 0.5, 0.85]:
    axes[0].annotate("", xy=(0.5 + (xp-0.5)*0.6, 0.25), xytext=(xp, 0.35),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
axes[0].set_xlim(0,1); axes[0].set_ylim(0,1); axes[0].axis("off")

axes[1].set_title("AdaBoost (sequential)")
xs = [0.1, 0.35, 0.6, 0.85]
for i, xp in enumerate(xs):
    axes[1].add_patch(plt.Rectangle((xp-0.08, 0.5), 0.16, 0.25,
                                    fc="#ffe6b3", ec="k", alpha=0.4+0.15*i))
    axes[1].text(xp, 0.625, f"stump {i+1}\nα{i+1}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
    if i < len(xs)-1:
        axes[1].annotate("", xy=(xs[i+1]-0.08, 0.625), xytext=(xp+0.08, 0.625),
                         arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
axes[1].add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0.35, 0.05), 0.3, 0.2, fc="#cfe8ff", ec="k"))
axes[1].text(0.5, 0.15, "weighted vote", ha="center", va="center")
axes[1].annotate("", xy=(0.5, 0.25), xytext=(xs[-1], 0.5),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
axes[1].set_xlim(0,1); axes[1].set_ylim(0,1); axes[1].axis("off")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-alpha-curve
#| fig-cap: "Stump weight α as a function of its weighted error ε. Better stumps (lower ε) get larger α."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5

eps = np.linspace(0.01, 0.49, 200)
alpha = 0.5*np.log((1-eps)/eps)
plt.figure(figsize=(5,3.5))
plt.plot(eps, alpha, lw=2)
plt.xlabel("stump weighted error ε"); plt.ylabel("stump weight α")
plt.title("AdaBoost: better stumps get larger α")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Data Prep

The labeled dataset is saved as [`data/clean/adaboost_data.csv`](data/clean/adaboost_data.csv).
It contains one row per company-year with the raw SEC fields (`Revenue`, `NetIncome`, `TotalAssets`, `TotalLiabilities`, `TotalEquity`, `LongTermDebt`, `OperatingIncome`, `CashFromOperations`), the derived ratios (`ROA`, `ROE`, `Debt_to_Equity`, `Profit_Margin`),
one engineered feature (`log_Assets`), and the binary target `HighROA`.
Rows with missing in any of `Debt_to_Equity`, `Profit_Margin`, `log_Assets`, `ROA`, or `sector` were dropped before saving.

```{python}
#| label: save-adaboost-data
#| echo: false

df = pd.read_csv("data/clean/company_financials_clean.csv")
df = df.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
df["log_Assets"] = np.log1p(df["TotalAssets"])
df = df.dropna(subset=["Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin","log_Assets","ROA","sector"]).copy()

train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
thr = train["ROA"].median()
train = train.copy(); test = test.copy()
train["HighROA"] = (train["ROA"] > thr).astype(int)
test["HighROA"]  = (test["ROA"]  > thr).astype(int)

full_labeled = pd.concat([train, test]).sort_index()
full_labeled.to_csv("data/clean/adaboost_data.csv", index=False)
train.to_csv("data/clean/train_adaboost.csv", index=False)
test.to_csv("data/clean/test_adaboost.csv",  index=False)
#print(f"Saved {len(full_labeled)} labeled rows | train = {len(train)} | test = {len(test)} | threshold = {thr:.4f}")
```

- **Two-class label: `HighROA`.** `HighROA = 1` if `ROA` > the **training-set median** ROA, and `0` otherwise.
The threshold is computed *after* the split, from training rows only.

The feature columns used by the model are `Debt_to_Equity`, `Profit_Margin`, `log_Assets`, and `sector`.

The labeled data is split 80/20 with `random_state=42`, giving roughly 32 training rows and 8 test rows for the 40-row sample.
The two sets are shown side by side below:

```{python}
#| label: fig-split-ada
#| fig-cap: "Training set (left) and testing set (right). Each company-year row appears in exactly one of the two sets — the sets are disjoint."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

train = pd.read_csv("data/clean/train_adaboost.csv")
test  = pd.read_csv("data/clean/test_adaboost.csv")
cols_show = ["ticker","fiscal_year","ROA","Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin","log_Assets","sector","HighROA"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
for ax, d, name in [(axes[0], train, "Training set"), (axes[1], test, "Testing set")]:
    ax.axis("off"); ax.set_title(f"{name} (n={len(d)})")
    t = ax.table(cellText=d[cols_show].head(8).round(3).values,
                 colLabels=cols_show, loc="center", cellLoc="center")
    t.auto_set_font_size(False); t.set_fontsize(7); t.scale(1, 1.4)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The two split files are linked here: [`data/clean/train_adaboost.csv`](data/clean/train_adaboost.csv) and [`data/clean/test_adaboost.csv`](data/clean/test_adaboost.csv).

`train_test_split` assigns each row to exactly one of the two sets, so no company-year observation appears in both.
They must be disjoint because the test set is meant to simulate companies the model has never seen.

`AdaBoostClassifier` in scikit-learn only accepts numeric inputs. So one-hot encoding via
`OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")` was used for `sector` columns 
that holds strings like `"Technology"` and `"Financials"`.
```{python}
#| label: fig-onehot-ada
#| fig-cap: "Left: the training data as loaded, with `sector` as a string column. Right: the same rows after one-hot encoding, with every input column numeric and ready for AdaBoost."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

num, cat = ["Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin","log_Assets"], ["sector"]
pre = ColumnTransformer([("num","passthrough",num),
                         ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat)])
X_enc = pre.fit_transform(train[num+cat])
colnames = num + list(pre.named_transformers_["cat"].get_feature_names_out(cat))
encoded = pd.DataFrame(X_enc, columns=colnames)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 5))
axes[0].axis("off"); axes[0].set_title("Before: sector is a string")
t0 = axes[0].table(cellText=train[["Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin","log_Assets","sector"]].head(6).round(3).values,
                   colLabels=["Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin","log_Assets","sector"],
                   loc="center", cellLoc="center")
t0.auto_set_font_size(False); t0.set_fontsize(8); t0.scale(1, 1.5)

axes[1].axis("off"); axes[1].set_title("After: all numeric (one-hot)")
t1 = axes[1].table(cellText=encoded.head(6).round(3).values,
                   colLabels=[c.replace("sector_","") for c in colnames],
                   loc="center", cellLoc="center")
t1.auto_set_font_size(False); t1.set_fontsize(7); t1.scale(1, 1.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

#print(f"Original feature columns: {num + cat}")
#print(f"Encoded feature columns ({len(colnames)}): {colnames}")
```

After encoding, the input matrix has `{python} len(colnames)` columns — three numeric plus one binary column per sector.

## Code

The Python script is saved at [`code/adaboost_model.py`](code/adaboost_model.py).

```{python}
#| label: fit-adaboost

train = pd.read_csv("data/clean/train_adaboost.csv")
test  = pd.read_csv("data/clean/test_adaboost.csv")

num = ["Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin","log_Assets"]
cat = ["sector"]
pre = ColumnTransformer([("num","passthrough",num),
                         ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat)])

def make_ada(n, lr):
    return Pipeline([("pre", pre),
        ("m", AdaBoostClassifier(
            estimator=DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1),
            n_estimators=n, learning_rate=lr, random_state=42))])

tr, val = train_test_split(train, test_size=0.25, random_state=1,
                           stratify=train["HighROA"])
rounds = [10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400]
accs = {lr: [] for lr in [0.1, 0.5, 1.0]}
for lr in accs:
    for n in rounds:
        m = make_ada(n, lr).fit(tr[num+cat], tr["HighROA"])
        accs[lr].append(accuracy_score(val["HighROA"], m.predict(val[num+cat])))

best = max(((lr, n) for lr in accs for n in rounds),
           key=lambda t: accs[t[0]][rounds.index(t[1])])
print("best (learning_rate, n_estimators) =", best)

final = make_ada(best[1], best[0]).fit(train[num+cat], train["HighROA"])
pred = final.predict(test[num+cat])
cm = confusion_matrix(test["HighROA"], pred)
acc = accuracy_score(test["HighROA"], pred)
#print("AdaBoost test accuracy =", round(acc, 4))
#print("Confusion matrix:\n", cm)
```

## Results

```{python}
#| label: fit-and-score-ada
#| echo: false

train = pd.read_csv("data/clean/train_adaboost.csv")
test  = pd.read_csv("data/clean/test_adaboost.csv")

num, cat = ["Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin","log_Assets"], ["sector"]
pre = ColumnTransformer([("num","passthrough",num),
                         ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat)])

def make_ada(n, lr):
    return Pipeline([("pre", pre),
        ("m", AdaBoostClassifier(
            estimator=DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1),
            n_estimators=n, learning_rate=lr, random_state=42))])

tr, val = train_test_split(train, test_size=0.25, random_state=1,
                           stratify=train["HighROA"])
rounds = [10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400]
accs = {lr: [] for lr in [0.1, 0.5, 1.0]}
for lr in accs:
    for n in rounds:
        m = make_ada(n, lr).fit(tr[num+cat], tr["HighROA"])
        accs[lr].append(accuracy_score(val["HighROA"], m.predict(val[num+cat])))

best = max(((lr, n) for lr in accs for n in rounds),
           key=lambda t: accs[t[0]][rounds.index(t[1])])

final = make_ada(best[1], best[0]).fit(train[num+cat], train["HighROA"])
pred = final.predict(test[num+cat])
cm   = confusion_matrix(test["HighROA"], pred)
acc  = accuracy_score(test["HighROA"], pred)
```

**Accuracy.** Test accuracy = **`{python} f"{acc:.4f}"`** on `{python} len(test)` test companies.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ada-confusion
#| fig-cap: "Confusion matrix for AdaBoost on the test set."
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4,3))
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt="d", cmap="Greens", ax=ax,
            xticklabels=["Pred 0","Pred 1"], yticklabels=["True 0","True 1"])
ax.set_title(f"AdaBoost confusion matrix (acc={acc:.3f})")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Tuning rounds and learning rate.** The plot below shows validation accuracy for `n_estimators ∈ {10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400}`
at learning rates {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}. The best setting was `n_estimators = 25`, `learning_rate = 0.1`.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ada-rounds
#| fig-cap: "Validation accuracy of AdaBoost as a function of the number of rounds, for three learning rates."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,4))
for lr, ys in accs.items():
    ax.plot(rounds, ys, marker="o", label=f"lr={lr}")
ax.set(xlabel="n_estimators (rounds)", ylabel="validation accuracy",
       title="AdaBoost: validation accuracy vs rounds")
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The single decision tree scored **0.583**; AdaBoost scored **`{python} f"{acc:.4f}"`**.
Both models performedd comparatively same on this dataset.

## (e) Conclusions

AdaBoost's test accuracy of **`{python} f"{acc:.4f}"`** is not a stable estimate because of the data size. The margin remains
the dominant feature, consistent with the linear and logistic results. Margin efficiency is the strongest green flag for
financial performance. Also, leverage is a much weaker signal than the "more debt means more risk" story would predict.
In summary, the effect of leverage and sector depends on the firm's margin profile.
